chapters.title: Chapter 5: Recent Shocks and the Investor's Playbook

lessons.title: IL&FS and the 2018 NBFC Crisis in India

body.text: A AAA rating is an opinion, not a guarantee. IL&FS carried the highest possible rating until August 2018, and within weeks it was in default, dragging India's entire shadow banking sector into a crisis.

children.text: Until August 2018, IL&FS bonds and loans were rated AAA, the same grade Indian rating agencies give the safest borrowers in the country. The group built roads, power plants and urban infrastructure through a web of more than 250 group companies. On 16 August 2018, CARE Ratings cut the rating on a key subsidiary's debt. By 8 September, ICRA had downgraded IL&FS loans and debentures to junk. In between, the group had started missing payments.

Chapter 1 used the DHFL share crash of September 2018 to explain contagion. This lesson tells the full story: how India's non-bank lenders grew, why IL&FS failed, how the stress spread to DHFL and PMC Bank, and the rules India rewrote so it would not happen again.

body.caption: The NBFC crisis on the five-stage map

cells: Build-up
While banks struggle with bad loans, NBFCs expand rapidly, funding long-term loans with short-term borrowing bought largely by mutual funds
Trigger
IL&FS, a AAA-rated infrastructure lender, misses payments and is downgraded to junk in August and September 2018
Panic and recognition
Mutual funds and banks pull back from NBFCs, funding costs jump, and hidden problems surface at DHFL and PMC Bank
Policy response
The government takes over the IL&FS board, SEBI and the RBI tighten rules, and a partial credit guarantee helps sound NBFCs raise money
Repair and recovery
DHFL becomes the first finance company resolved under the IBC, NBFCs face bank-like liquidity rules, and IL&FS repays creditors over several years

children.text: Build-up: The Rise of India's Shadow Banks

Non-banking financial companies lend like banks but cannot take ordinary current and savings deposits. As you saw in Chapter 1, Lesson 3, Indian public sector banks spent the mid-2010s buried under bad loans. NBFCs and housing finance companies stepped into the gap, lending aggressively for homes, vehicles, real estate projects and infrastructure.

The problem was how they funded that growth. Many borrowed through short-term commercial paper, much of it bought by liquid and other debt mutual funds, and used it to fund loans lasting 10, 15 or 20 years. This is an
asset-liability mismatch

markDefs.definition: When a lender's assets, such as loans, pay back over a much longer period than its liabilities, such as borrowings, fall due. It works only as long as the lender can keep refinancing its short-term debt.

body.title: Measure the Funding Gap
body.prompt: Using the table above, how much new borrowing, in ₹ crore, must the NBFC raise over the next 12 months to meet its repayments, after using all its incoming loan repayments and its liquid assets?
body.explanation: Money due out: ₹6,000 crore. Money available: ₹2,000 crore of loan repayments plus ₹500 crore of liquid assets, or ₹2,500 crore. The gap is ₹6,000 crore minus ₹2,500 crore, which is ₹3,500 crore of fresh borrowing. In normal times, that is routine. When mutual funds stop buying NBFC paper, as they did in late 2018, the same gap can push a profitable lender into default.

children.text: Trigger: How a AAA Group Fell

IL&FS was not a small, obscure lender. It was one of India's best-known infrastructure financiers, backed by blue-chip institutional shareholders. Its structure, however, made trouble hard to see from outside.
Infrastructure projects take many years to generate cash, but group companies had borrowed heavily, including short-term.
Money was raised at the holding company and at financing arms, then lent onward to project companies across the group.
Stalled and delayed projects meant cash did not come back as planned.
The group relied on fresh borrowing to repay old borrowing, the rollover trap from Chapter 1.
When lenders hesitated in 2018, the group could not refinance and began missing payments.

body.title: What the AAA rating signalled vs what was inside

columns.label: What the rating implied
points: The highest degree of safety for timely repayment
Suitable for conservative debt funds and treasuries

columns.label: What turned out to be true
points: A group already struggling to refinance its debt
A complex web of more than 250 entities with money moving between them
Shareholders who were not obliged to cover the group's debts
Governance and accounting problems later placed under investigation

body.text: Ratings lag reality. Agencies moved IL&FS from AAA to junk in roughly a month, which means the rating was telling investors very little about the real risk until it was too late to act. A rating is a starting point for your own questions, not a replacement for them.

children.text: Panic: The Crisis Spreads

body.title: From IL&FS to a new rulebook

events.title: The first downgrade
events.description: CARE Ratings downgrades debentures of IL&FS Financial Services, the group's main lending arm.

events.title: Defaults and junk ratings
events.description: IL&FS misses repayments, including a ₹1,000 crore short-term loan from SIDBI. ICRA downgrades its loans and debentures to junk on 8 September.

events.title: Contagion reaches DHFL
events.description: A distressed sale of DHFL commercial paper sends its shares down about 42% in a day, as covered in Chapter 1.

events.title: Government takes control
events.description: The NCLT allows the government to replace the IL&FS board with a new one including banker Uday Kotak.

events.title: SEBI allows side pockets
events.description: Mutual funds are permitted to separate downgraded debt into a segregated portfolio to protect other investors.

events.title: DHFL defaults
events.description: The housing finance company begins missing payments on its bonds.

events.title: Budget support for NBFCs
events.description: The Union Budget announces a partial credit guarantee so public sector banks can buy up to ₹1 lakh crore of high-rated pooled assets from sound NBFCs.

events.title: Safer liquid funds
events.description: SEBI requires liquid funds to hold at least 20% in cash and cash-like assets such as government securities and treasury bills.

events.title: PMC Bank frozen
events.description: The RBI restricts Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative Bank and initially caps withdrawals at ₹1,000 per customer.

events.title: Liquidity rules for NBFCs
events.description: The RBI requires large NBFCs to hold high-quality liquid assets to survive 30 days of stress, phased in from December 2020.

events.title: DHFL goes to the IBC
events.description: The RBI supersedes DHFL's board, making it the first financial services company referred for insolvency under the IBC.

events.title: DHFL resolved
events.description: Piramal completes its takeover of DHFL, paying about ₹34,250 crore to creditors.

events.title: Scale-based regulation
events.description: The RBI announces a framework that regulates NBFCs more strictly as they grow larger and riskier, effective from 1 October 2022.

children.text: PMC Bank: When One Borrower Is the Whole Bank

The PMC Bank collapse was not caused by IL&FS, but it came out of the same period of hidden stress. PMC, an urban co-operative bank, had lent more than ₹6,500 crore to real estate developer HDIL and its group, about 73% of its total advances. The RBI found the bank had hidden and misreported those loans. When HDIL collapsed, so did PMC.

body.title: How Much Was Actually Insured?
body.question: When the RBI froze PMC Bank in September 2019, how much of each depositor's money was covered by DICGC deposit insurance?
options: The full deposit, with no limit
Nothing, because co-operative banks are not covered
body.explanation: The cover in September 2019 was ₹1 lakh per depositor per bank, a limit that had not changed in decades. Co-operative banks are covered by DICGC, but many PMC depositors had far more than ₹1 lakh in the bank, and withdrawals were initially capped at ₹1,000. In February 2020, a few months later, the cover was raised to ₹5 lakh, the limit you learnt about in Chapter 1.

body.text: PMC is the classic concentration failure. Chapter 2 showed how thousands of small US banks failed in the 1930s partly because they were tied to local farm economies. PMC tied almost three quarters of its lending to a single borrower group. No amount of good lending elsewhere can save a bank from that.

children.text: Policy Response: Rewriting the Rules
The NBFC crisis led to one of the biggest rounds of rule changes in Indian finance since 1991, spread across the government, SEBI and the RBI.

body.title: Show me how a side pocket protects investors

children.text: Suppose a debt fund has ₹1,000 crore of assets and 10 crore units, so its NAV is ₹100 per unit. It holds ₹50 crore of bonds from a company that has just defaulted.

cells: The bond defaults
The fund marks the ₹50 crore bond down, so the NAV falls
The defaulted bond is moved into a separate segregated portfolio
Nervous investors redeem
Early exiters leave at the reduced NAV, and remaining investors bear any extra losses from forced selling
Everyone keeps units in both the main portfolio and the segregated portfolio
Money is later recovered
Investors who already left get nothing from the recovery
Recoveries are paid to everyone who held units on the day of segregation

children.text: Side pockets do not make the loss disappear. They share it fairly and stop a rush to exit that punishes the investors who stay.

body.title: The NAV Hit
body.prompt: In the example above, the fund has ₹1,000 crore of assets and 10 crore units. If the ₹50 crore defaulted bond is written down to zero, what is the new NAV per unit in the main portfolio, in ₹?
body.explanation: Remaining assets = ₹1,000 crore minus ₹50 crore = ₹950 crore. NAV = ₹950 crore ÷ 10 crore units = ₹95 per unit, a 5% fall. With a side pocket, each investor also holds segregated units that would pay out if any of the ₹50 crore is later recovered.

body.title: Name the Trap
body.textWithBlank: An NBFC that funds 15-year home loans with commercial paper due in 3 months has an asset-liability ___.
body.explanation: An asset-liability mismatch. It was the core weakness of India's NBFC boom, and it is why the RBI later required large NBFCs to hold liquidity buffers.

children.text: Repair: Where Things Stand

Resolution has been slow but real. DHFL was taken over by Piramal in 2021, with creditors receiving about ₹34,250 crore. IL&FS has sold assets, transferred road projects into an infrastructure investment trust and repaid creditors in stages. By June 2026, it had repaid ₹50,387 crore, about 82.6% of its ₹61,000 crore resolution target, against total external debt of ₹99,377 crore. Creditors will not get all their money back.

body.title: The 9.5% NBFC Fixed Deposit
body.scenario: A mid-sized NBFC advertises a 3-year fixed deposit at 9.5%, well above what large banks offer. It has a AA rating, has grown its loan book 40% a year for three years, lends mostly to real estate developers, and funds itself heavily with commercial paper. Your relative wants to put ₹10 lakh into it.
body.prompt: Using the lessons of 2018, what would you check before investing, and what would worry you most here?
body.modelAnswer: First, understand what the extra yield is paying for. A rate well above bank FDs means the market sees more risk, and unlike a bank deposit, an NBFC deposit is not covered by DICGC insurance. Then check: one, the asset-liability profile in the annual report or disclosures, especially how much borrowing is due within a year compared with loans maturing and liquid assets held. Heavy reliance on commercial paper is exactly the IL&FS and DHFL pattern. Two, concentration: lending mostly to real estate developers is a sector bet, and the PMC lesson shows what happens when too much sits with one sector or group. Three, growth: 40% a year for three years is fast, and rapid growth can hide weak lending until the cycle turns. Four, the rating trend and the rating rationale, not just the letter grade, remembering that IL&FS was AAA weeks before default. Five, the NBFC's regulatory layer under the RBI's scale-based framework and whether it meets liquidity requirements. Six, group structure and related-party lending. What worries most: short-term funding plus concentrated real estate lending plus rapid growth, which is close to the 2018 recipe. Even if the NBFC is sound, putting ₹10 lakh in a single uninsured deposit concentrates your own risk. Splitting across safer options, or limiting the amount, is the lesson from PMC depositors.

body.title: Before You Lend to an NBFC, Directly or Through a Debt Fund
steps: Check how much of its borrowing is short-term, especially commercial paper, compared with its liquid assets
Look for concentration in one sector, borrower group or geography
Read the rating rationale and watch for any rating outlook turning negative, not just the rating letter
For a debt fund, open the monthly portfolio disclosure and note exposure to lower rated and NBFC paper
Check whether the fund can create segregated portfolios, and whether it has done so before
Remember that NBFC deposits and debt funds are not covered by DICGC deposit insurance

body.label: AMFI: Mutual Fund Portfolio Disclosures
body.description: The Association of Mutual Funds in India website links to fund houses and industry data. Use it, together with each AMC's monthly portfolio disclosure, to see exactly which NBFCs and companies your debt fund lends to.

points: India's NBFCs grew rapidly while banks struggled with bad loans, funding long-term loans with short-term commercial paper bought largely by mutual funds
IL&FS, rated AAA until August 2018, defaulted and was downgraded to junk within weeks, with group debt of about ₹91,000 crore
The stress spread through mutual funds and funding markets to DHFL, while PMC Bank collapsed after lending about 73% of its advances to a single group
Reforms followed: side pockets, stricter liquid fund rules, a partial credit guarantee, liquidity rules for NBFCs, IBC resolution for finance companies and scale-based regulation
Resolution has been slow: DHFL was sold to Piramal for about ₹34,250 crore, and IL&FS had repaid ₹50,387 crore by June 2026

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The NBFC, fund and fixed deposit examples are hypothetical, and no company, fund or deposit is being recommended or criticised. Historical figures are drawn from RBI, SEBI, Government of India, company disclosures and news reports, and some are still subject to ongoing legal and resolution processes.
